draft.title: Using critics well
card: A critic is a scholar or reviewer who has written an interpretation of a text. Quoting or referring to a critic can support your argument or sharpen it.
Your own reading of the text must lead. The thesis and the main analysis are yours, and the critic's view comes in to serve them.
Treat a critic's view as evidence to test. Check it against the text, then say whether it fits, and where it does not, explain why.
A critic's quotation cannot stand in for analysis. If a paragraph is mostly a critic's words with little comment from you, the analysis is missing.
draft.remember: Let your own reading lead, and test a critic's view against the text before you use it.

a.q: Which use of a critic in an essay paragraph is the strongest?
opts: Quoting a critic, then testing the view against the text
Opening with a critic so their view makes the main point
Using a critic's quotation in place of analysis of the text
Listing three critics and leaving out your own reading
a.why: The strongest use treats the critic's view as evidence and tests it against the text, so the student's reading leads. The other options let the critic replace or crowd out the student's own analysis.
a.clue: Who should lead the argument, and what is done to the critic's view?

b.q: Leila argues that the narrator of a novel is unreliable. She quotes a critic who agrees, then moves straight on without commenting. What should she do to use the critic well?
opts: Show how a moment in the text proves the claim, in her words
Add a second critic who agrees to make the claim look firmer
Drop her own point, since a critic has already made it
Move the quotation to the start so the critic's voice leads
b.why: The critic's view is evidence, so Leila needs to link it to the text and add her own analysis. A second critic only adds more quotation, and the critic's claim should not take the place of her own reading.
b.clue: A quotation on its own is not analysis, so what has Leila not yet done?
